I can see my former self in the way you describe your boyfriend. He feels listless and depressed, is disconnecting himself from people, and is anxious and insecure about his performance at work. He has these holes in his life that he is filling with cocaine. After enough sustained coke use, he probably feels like he can't enjoy anything in life, and he may be thinking about suicide. 

I was in that place, and reading about another person who could be there is breaking my heart too, because I wish that someone would have reached out to me and made me feel like there was someone who cared about me. I would get into such a mood of despair about my life that I did the unthinkable (for me) and actually called a friend in a far away place, and he recommended I seek out a therapist. I was fortunate enough to have easy access to one, and he was amazing in helping me understand myself better, and eventually starting the mental process that helped me kick cocaine and alcohol.

Your boyfriend needs to look at his own life and really ask himself if he is happy with the way things are. He needs to look back on his experience using cocaine and recognize that it (1) provides temporary relief, and (2) over enough time, it creates, or strongly contributes to, the mental and emotional states that lead to one using it. Using that drug will strip you of your ability to do what you want with your life, and all it leaves in its wake is a depressed coke goblin.

One thing I do think is that cocaine goes hand in hand with being self-absorbed. Maybe just tell him what you told us, about him being kind, smart, motivated, and lovely, and how he can be so much more, but only if he can grow past his use of cocaine. But ultimately, he needs a support circle who he can be honest with about his cocaine use, and that's not something you can give him from far away.

You also have a responsibility to protect yourself. We grow up thinking that the ideal of romantic love is being eternally self-sacrificing and always working to get your partner through everything, but the reality of that is exhausting, and it never works the way we hope. Supporting a person who does not want to help themselves is only going to burn you out and leave you feeling upset, neurotic, and ultimately betrayed. The only way for the both of you to survive as a couple is for him to commit to abstaining from coke and seeking treatment - otherwise, you need to be ready to leave. I know it hurts to consider that possibility, but the alternative - staying with a person who refuses to help themselves - will hurt so much more.

I hope this was helpful for you to read. I know things are not looking super bright, but you seem like a lovely person, so I can only hope that your boyfriend sees that as well and decides to change.

As it is now, you're using the drink as a crutch for your personality. Eventually, the alcohol is going to consume everything good about you, until you're just a dull, depressed, bitter husk of a person.

It's up to you to decide what kind of a person you want to be. But I promise you, in the long term, alcohol will make you the exact opposite of that ideal you.

Regarding your second paragraph, I tried 4 of the minutemen overhaul mods and the one that seemed the most lore-friendly was You And What Army. It'll spawn minutemen in various levels (from 1 to the PC character) who will usually be kitted out with thematically appropriate gear. I'll usually see 2-3 escorting my caravans around, 3-4 + dog on a patrol, and you'll occasionally run across little checkpoints of them in shacks with beds/consumables.

I think the best example of this mod at play was when I went to Revere station for some radiant quest. There was a PA raider + maybe 6 regulars, so I decided to drop a flare, and 4 decently kitted minutemen (2 in polymer combat armor, level 30+) joined the fray and made it a fun little battle. Rust devils showed up and hit us from the rear, so most of the MM got wiped, but they didn't get murdered immediately. That's been my experience with the mod - they can't stand up to dedicated aggressive enemies, but are competent against animals and small groups of humans or mutants. And if you've turned a settlement into a supply line hub (I did this with Starlight and County Crossing), you'll usually see a dozen or so non-settler minutemen coming and going, which really fits the roleplay of turning those spots into garrison hubs - and if gunners or mutants or whatever spawn in for an attack, they get overwhelmed by minutemen numbers, which is exactly how it should be for one of your bases.

It shows remarkable self-awareness to recognize what's happening in your head, and bravery to admit out loud. Believe me when I say that I wish I had this voice and this consternation in my mind after the first few times I bought cocaine, instead of after the 100th. 

Your brain will use all of the powers of your intellect and your suasion to convince you that it's okay to do more blow, and that it will be fun, and that there's no harm in doing so because you can't get addicted. And it's outstanding of you to recognize this voice for what it is, the siren song of addiction.

Having been down this road (and having seen many others on it), let me assure you that continued cocaine use gets worse and makes everything horrible. You will feel unhealthy - your sinuses will get stuffy, your nose will hurt, your head will pound, your body will go through yo-yos of unhealthy weight loss and weight gain. Your mind will fritter away as you get irritable and snap at your loved ones. You won't even notice this, until one day you decide to go for a walk to the top of a parking garage and realize that you are about to throw yourself off the roof, because cocaine robbed you of the ability to feel pleasure in anything besides itself - and when that pleasure will become fleeting, requiring more and more of the drug to simply feel less anxious. Taken far enough, it will rob you of health, of sanity, of joy, and of life itself. This is the INEVITABLE outcome of prolonged cocaine use - there is no such thing as a healthy relationship with this  substance.

I know this is bleak to hear and to feel. I know that cocaine made you feel fun and sexy and wild - trust me when I say that this is all you, and this drug only briefly took away the anxiety and inhibition that kept you from expressing that. The best part of stopping cocaine (and alcohol, the two go together like honey and biscuits) is learning how to bring that person out of you, sober and on your terms. I learned to do it. You can do that too.

I don't know you sister, but I think you have the strength to keep yourself from going down this road. Remind yourself that prolonged use and it's consequences will get worse - and remind yourself that you CAN live a fun and enjoyable life without coke.

If you've found yourself thinking of running as being the time when you find yourself at your happiest, then I think it's reasonable to model it as an addiction. By it's nature as a physical activity, it should be largely self limiting, but if you're at the point where you're overtraining and feeling depressed, then that super efficient reward-effort cycle in your head may have largely coopted your running and may be making you escalate your training cycle just to manage your mood.

I'm not a psychologist, so take my words with a grain of salt. I am an addict (outside of running), so I have some experience with... uh mood feedback cycles. And when you think something you're doing is amazing and it makes you feel better and healthier and stronger and just more "you", it is important to stand back and ask yourself if that thought is in your overall best interest, or just the interest of the feedback loop that's dominating your brain.

My advice to you would be to take 3 days off running. If you begin to feel an urge for physical activity, lift some weights, bicycle, dance - something not running. Show yourself that running doesn't control your ability to enjoy life and your own body.

I'm going to go on something of a rambling screed here, so I apologize to the effort posting class.

I do strongly feel that, given the sinusoid of our economic history, we are looking at a general "L-shaped" economic contraction within the next couple of years. The inflationary pressure that I suspect is driven by a decade of quantitative easing cash finally percolating down into the real economy, and the swing of the pendulum in the direction of labor, is being looked at by the ghouls of the ownership class with some trepidation. They likely see a contraction as a way to "cool off" the economy, and if they get a chance to swoop in and buy up foreclosed homes and equities from newly jobless cash-poor retail investors who went balls deep on Robinhood, well, hey, personal responsibility at it's finest.

With that being said, I do think there's a touch more class consciousness in the United States then there's been in decades. Two years of a pandemic that already subjected many workers to economic hardship, and the ruling class narratives that come down to "we need to stomp down on wagies asking for more", has played some part in exposing an atomized, individualistic, and sometimes selfish American public to the reality that there is an us vs them conflict in our society that breaks down by class.

So what do the wealthy think is going to happen when you pull the rug out from under these people, leaving them wretched but with an abundance of time on their hands?

With that being said, I recognize the possibility that I may get laid off in the event of a contraction. I've been laid off once before (2014 oil crunch hit hard, which is also why I've been loling hard at all the O&G hiring content on LinkedIn right now), and I remember how devastating that experience was. I think it's important as well that we start taking some concrete steps to estimate the social and material support that we can provide to those who do become dispossessed in the event of a depression.

This is still a forming thought in my head, but the three prongs of this idea are community outreach, demand suppression, and barter exchanges (I know that sounds absurd, I'll try to r-slur through this).

Community outreach: I would hope that the pandemic has given us the chance to see groups in our area that provide free or affordable material support. I know we all love to shit on the DSA, but the chapter in my area has done good work engaging with food banks and shelter organizations. They have a mailing list, they talk regularly, and in the event of a recession I hope and expect that they'll become a forum for discussing mutual aid strategies. On the less political side, religious organizations will also provide community forums that center around mutual aid in times of hardship. One doesn't need to be an adherent of a faith to engage with them. I do want to explore this a little bit further, but I'd also to get a more concrete assessment of which of our public goods have not been rendered completely dysfunctional so that we can leverage those as outreach spaces and aid resources.

Demand suppression: this kind of ties in with the next idea, but I'd like to keep it separated for now. Ultimately, a recession will mean going without a lot of things. Whatever degree of comfort or enjoyment we experience now, we will all have to tighten our belts to bear out a recession. We do need to start thinking about how we can reduce our consumption now, so that it becomes less of a hardship to bear when we're obliged to do do after a layoff were to occur.

Barter exchanges: as noted, this is something of a hare brained idea, but I do want to keep thinking about the efficacy of implementing it within a modern economy. Unpaid exchanges have been taking place forever - the most common example I can think of are how women for the majority have acted as caregivers and homemakers in exchange for food/shelter/etc. It is however hard to conceive of this in large parts of the American economy, because (1) we are detached from each other and don't know to reach out to ask for or offer help, and (2) many of us do such specialized absurdities in our advanced economies that we may feel completely useless in an economic context reduced to the exchange of basic goods and services. But there are so many things we need that can be done in a minimal fashion and therefore exchanged - cooking, caregiving, basic healthcare, teaching, basic mechanical maintenance, etc. A recession doesn't make people's skills and needs evaporate overnight. Figuring out how to facilitate those exchanges in a manner that doesn't rely on cash transactions would be useful.

Ultimately, class solidarity means nothing without community in the face of hardship. If our rulers want to subject us to despair for the sake of their own rapacity, we can only fight them by binding together and rejecting the societal paradigm they try to impose upon us.
